analysis.one_liner: Directs the EPA to study combined pollution risks and fix chronic environmental-law violations in overburdened communities.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its initial committee referrals and received no cosponsors, dying without a vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Environmental Protection Agency to write and carry out a protocol for assessing the combined public health effects of multiple pollution sources and climate impacts at once, rather than one pollutant at a time [S3]. It would also require the EPA to identify at least 100 communities with above-average rates of environmental law violations that are disproportionately communities of color, low-income communities, or tribal communities, determine why the violations happen, and put fixes in place within two years [S3]. The bill was referred to two House committees in March 2023 and never moved further [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities that bear a disproportionate share of pollution and environmental violations, which the bill defines as communities with significant representation of people of color, low-income households, or tribal and indigenous populations [S3]. These residents would gain a formal EPA assessment of their combined exposures and a mandated plan to cut violations below the national average [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to publish, take public comment on, and implement a protocol assessing cumulative public health risks from multiple environmental stressors, including climate impacts like extreme heat, flooding, and wildfire and pollution regulated under the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and other laws [S3].

Requires the EPA to identify at least 100 environmental justice communities with more environmental-law violations than the national average over the previous five years, analyze the root causes with input from residents, and implement measures to bring violations significantly below the national average within two years [S3].
Mandates at least four public hearings on the proposed protocol, timed and located to maximize public input, giving affected residents a formal channel to weigh in [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Facilities that emit pollutants, discharge waste, or generate hazardous materials, which would face a regulatory regime that counts their combined effects and tougher enforcement in communities with high violation rates [S3]. Taxpayers would fund the EPA's expanded analysis and enforcement workload.

drawbacks.text: The bill directs regulatory analysis and enforcement without providing new funding, so the EPA would have to absorb the cost of a 100-community study, a national protocol, and added enforcement measures within tight statutory deadlines [S3].

Industry groups generally argue cumulative-impact protocols create permitting uncertainty and compliance costs that can slow projects and raise prices; the bill gives EPA discretion over how strict the protocol is, which businesses would bear through compliance spending [S3].

Deadlines are ambitious, requiring a final protocol within one year and full implementation of fixes in 100 communities within two years of enactment, timelines that regulators and affected state agencies could struggle to meet [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of heavily polluted communities, the potential benefit is meaningful: an official accounting of their combined exposures and a federal mandate to fix chronic violations. The costs fall mainly on regulated facilities and federal and state agencies' workloads, and the bill's tight deadlines and lack of dedicated funding make its implementation plan harder than its goals. The design is reasonable in intent but under-resourced; in any case, it never advanced far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees in spring 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette (D-CO) introduced the bill on March 21, 2023, with no cosponsors [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Natural Resources Committee [S5].

In late March and April 2023 it was referred to the Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials Subcommittee and the Indian and Insular Affairs Subcommittee, and no further action of any kind appears in the record [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, having never reached a committee vote or the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that emit or discharge pollutants are better off because the bill died: no cumulative-impact protocol or mandated enforcement surge in high-violation communities was ever imposed. Residents of overburdened communities remain without the federal cumulative-risk assessment the bill would have required.

for.name: Diana DeGette
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor; it drew no cosponsors during the Congress [S1].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of first referral (Republican majority in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 2023 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; its Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials Subcommittee took no further action [S5].

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral (Republican majority in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 2023; its Indian and Insular Affairs Subcommittee took no further action and the bill never advanced [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.industry: Industrial polluters (emitters, dischargers, and waste handlers)
industries.note: The bill would have required the EPA to assess their combined pollution effects together and intensify enforcement in communities with high violation rates, raising compliance and enforcement exposure [S3]. Their gain from the bill's failure is continued one-pollutant-at-a-time regulation and the enforcement status quo in overburdened communities [S3].

industries.industry: Fossil fuel and heavy industry sectors exposed to climate-linked regulation
industries.note: The proposed protocol explicitly includes climate impacts such as extreme heat, drought, flooding, and storms as stressors to be weighed in permitting and enforcement analysis [S3]. The bill's death leaves existing regulatory practice in place.
